title: Why Semantic HTML Matters 🌟
description: Discover how meaningful tags improve accessibility, SEO, and maintainability.

slides.title: What Does 'Semantic' Really Mean? 🧠
slides.content:
# Tags That Describe Their Content

A semantic element clearly describes its meaning to both the browser and the developer.

- **Non‑semantic:** `<div>` and `<span>` tell nothing about their content.
- **Semantic:** `<nav>`, `<article>`, `<footer>` explicitly state their purpose.

Think of it like this: a `<div>` is a plain cardboard box with no label. A `<nav>` is a box labelled "Navigation". The label helps everyone understand what's inside.

slides.title: Benefits for Accessibility ♿
slides.content:
# Helping Assistive Technologies

Screen readers and other assistive tools rely on semantic landmarks to navigate pages. For example, a screen reader can jump straight to `<main>` or `<nav>` if they're properly marked.

Without semantics, a user might have to tab through dozens of generic `<div>` elements. With semantics, they can skip to the content they need.

Semantics are not just a luxury – they're essential for inclusive design.

quizData.question: Which of the following is a semantic HTML element?
quizData.explanation: <article> carries meaning (self‑contained composition); <div> and <span> are generic.

slides.title: SEO: Search Engines Love Structure 🔍
slides.content:
# Better Rankings with Meaningful Markup

Search engines analyze your HTML to understand content hierarchy. Semantic tags like `<h1>`, `<article>`, `<section>` help them index your page correctly.

A well‑structured page with a single `<h1>`, logical heading levels, and appropriate landmarks is more likely to appear in relevant search results. It's like giving Google a map instead of a maze.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Treat `<div>` as a Last Resort

Before using a `<div>`, ask yourself: "Is there a semantic element that matches the purpose of this container?" If yes, use it!
